strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical question in SAE research: how to select the L0 hyperparameter, which is commonly treated as a neutral design choice via sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff plots. The finding that this framing is actively misleading is valuable.

The toy model with ground-truth features provides a clean causal demonstration that MSE loss incentivizes low-L0 SAEs to learn incorrect, polysemantic latents (the learned SAE achieves better MSE than the ground-truth SAE). This is a crisp and convincing result with clear implications for SAE evaluation methodology.

The proposed Nth decoder projection metric is simple, cheap to compute, and novel. The paper shows it consistently identifies the same L0 range (200-250) on Gemma-2-2b across many choices of n, and this prediction is independently validated by peak performance on the sparse probing benchmark of Kantamneni et al.

The experiments probing L0 transitions during training (Appendix A.3) reveal an interesting asymmetry: SAEs starting at too-high L0 can recover when L0 is corrected, but too-low L0 creates a persistent local minimum. This has practical implications for SAE training schedules.

The analysis of open-source SAEs on Neuronpedia (Appendix A.5) grounds the work in current practice and gives actionable guidance to practitioners. Code is stated to be available, supporting reproducibility.
The limitations section is honest and specific, clearly scoping the findings to BatchTopK SAEs on a single model/layer.
weaknesses: The empirical base for the central claim ('most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low') is narrow: a single model (Gemma-2-2b), a single layer (layer 12), a single SAE width (32k), and a single architecture (BatchTopK). Extrapolating to all models, layers, widths, and architectures (JumpReLU, TopK, L1) is speculative, especially since the correct L0 likely depends on all of these factors.

The validation of the s_n^dec metric relies on agreement with the sparse probing benchmark, but peak sparse probing F1 is itself only a proxy for 'correct features,' not ground truth. Both metrics could share systematic confounds (e.g., both correlating with reconstruction variance explained at moderate L0). In the LLM setting there is no ground-truth feature check analogous to Figure 1.

The theoretical justification for why s_n^dec should be minimized exactly at the true L0 is informal and intuitive ('most latents should have near-zero projection on arbitrary training inputs'). The choice n = h/2 is described as empirical; a more principled derivation or sensitivity analysis of when the metric fails (e.g., highly anisotropic activations, heavy-tailed feature frequency distributions) would strengthen the claim.

The toy model uses mutually orthogonal features with a random correlation matrix and linearly decaying firing probabilities, which is a simplification. Real LLM feature distributions exhibit hierarchical/absorbing structure (as the authors' own related-work discussion of feature absorption notes), and it is unclear whether the low-L0 'cheating' pathology and the metric's behavior carry over to such structure.

No repeated seeds or variance estimates are reported for the LLM experiments, and the sparse probing F1 differences across L0 (Figure 4) are relatively small (~0.02-0.03), so it is hard to assess whether the peak at 200-250 is statistically meaningful.

The automatic L0 optimization procedure in Appendix A.4 is acknowledged by the authors to require substantial hyperparameter tuning and not to work reliably in real LLMs, which limits the practical utility of the otherwise promising metric; this should perhaps be more clearly flagged as exploratory.

The manuscript is very short (roughly 4 pages of main text), and some experiments that would substantially bolster the claims (e.g., a second model, a second layer, or a second architecture) appear to have been within reach given the toy-scale compute used elsewhere.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and under-examined question in SAE research: whether L0 is a neutral design choice or a hyperparameter with a 'correct' value, directly challenging the widely assumed sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff framing.

The toy model with ground-truth features and an explicit correlation structure allows a clean causal demonstration that (a) too-low L0 causes feature mixing and (b) MSE loss actively rewards incorrect, 'cheating' solutions (Section 3.1, Figures 1 and 6). The finding that a ground-truth-correct SAE scores *worse* on variance explained than corrupted SAEs is a striking and valuable result for the field.

The proposed Nth decoder projection metric is simple, cheap to compute, and its minimum is validated against an independent downstream signal (sparse probing F1 on Kantammeneni et al.'s benchmark), with the two agreeing at L0 ≈ 200-250 for Gemma-2-2b layer 12.
The transition experiments in Appendix A.3 (too-low L0 is a hard-to-escape local minimum, while too-high L0 is recoverable) add real insight beyond a static hyperparameter sweep.
The paper is clearly written, reproducible (code released, training details given), and includes an honest limitations section acknowledging the single-model, single-architecture scope.
weaknesses: Generality is overclaimed relative to the evidence. All LLM experiments use one model (Gemma-2-2b), one layer (12), one architecture (BatchTopK), and one SAE width (32k) trained on only 500M tokens. The sweeping claims that 'most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low' and that the sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff framing is broadly misleading rest largely on Neuropedia L0 histograms (Appendix A.5) for models whose correct L0 was never established. This is suggestive, not demonstrated.

The proposed metric has a circularity concern: the text states that 'n should be sufficiently larger than a reasonable guess at the correct L0' and that n ≈ h/2 works empirically. The metric's reliability therefore presupposes approximate knowledge of the quantity it is meant to discover, and the sensitivity of conclusions to this choice is explored only anecdotally (two toy settings, a grid of plots in A.7 with no quantitative analysis of minima locations).

No error bars, random seeds, or statistical uncertainty are reported anywhere. The s_n^dec curves (Figures 2, 3, 10) are visibly noisy and non-monotonic; the claim that minima 'match' the probing peak at 200-250 appears to rely on eyeballing broad, flat regions of both curves rather than a precise, quantified agreement.

Sparse probing F1 is an indirect proxy for 'correct features.' The paper never validates in the LLM setting that SAEs at L0=200-250 actually recover more ground-truth or more monosemantic features (e.g., via automated interpretability scoring or known feature circuits), so the link between the toy-model story (feature mixing) and the LLM observations remains correlational.

Alternative or standard baselines for hyperparameter selection are absent. The paper does not compare s_n^dec against other candidate selection signals (e.g., downstream task transfer, Ravel/Karvonen-style evaluations, or even the L1-vs-BatchTopK interaction), leaving its practical advantage unquantified.

The automatic L0-finding procedure in Appendix A.4 is admitted by the authors to work 'well in toy models' but require 'a lot of hyperparameter tuning to work in real LLMs,' weakening the practical payoff of the contribution; this failure should arguably be in the main text, not an appendix aside.

Toy-model design choices (50 orthogonal features, a single random correlation matrix, linearly decreasing firing probabilities, summed features) are reasonable but narrowly explored; no sensitivity analysis shows the low-L0 pathology persists across correlation structures or overcomplete regimes.

strengths: The toy model experiments with ground-truth features provide a clean and convincing demonstration of the central phenomenon: SAEs with too-low L0 learn latents that mix correlated features, and this is clearly visualized in Figure 1.

The finding that MSE loss actively prefers the 'cheating' SAE over the ground-truth dictionary at low L0 (Section 3.1, Appendix A.2) is a genuinely interesting result that challenges the standard sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff framing used across the SAE literature.

The proposed Nth decoder projection metric is validated against an independent downstream benchmark (sparse probing, Figure 4), and both converge on L0 ≈ 200–250, which lends credibility to the method.
The paper is well written and clearly organized, with hyperparameters, training details, and released code supporting reproducibility.

The paper includes an honest limitations section (A.6) that correctly identifies the restricted scope (one model, one layer, one architecture), and the appendix explores related phenomena (L0 transitions during training, open-source SAE survey) that add value.
weaknesses: Breadth of evidence is limited: all LLM results come from a single model (Gemma-2-2b), a single layer (12), a single architecture (BatchTopK), and a single dictionary width (32k). The sweeping claim that 'most SAEs used by researchers today have too low L0' is extrapolated from this narrow setting; how the optimal L0 varies with layer, model scale, and dictionary size is unknown and untested.

There is no ground truth for the correct L0 in LLMs. The paper validates the s_n^dec metric against sparse probing F1, but sparse probing is itself just one proxy for feature quality; agreement between two proxies does not establish that L0 ≈ 200–250 is truly 'correct.' The framing occasionally overstates this as identifying the true L0.

The s_n^dec metric and the choice of N (empirically 'up to about h/2') are heuristic, with no theoretical justification for why the metric should be minimized at the true L0 or why it should be robust across architectures and training scales.

The metric is only shown for BatchTopK SAEs where L0 is directly controlled; the claim that results would 'not be meaningfully different' for L1/JumpReLU SAEs is asserted rather than demonstrated, despite L1 SAEs being the dominant architecture in practice.

No variance reporting: plots appear to be from single training runs with no seeds, error bars, or statistical uncertainty, which is a concern given that the minimum of s_n^dec is read off a relatively flat curve.

The automatic L0-finding procedure in Appendix A.4 is acknowledged by the authors to work 'well in toy models' but requires substantial hyperparameter tuning and is not demonstrated on LLMs, limiting the practical impact of the main contribution.
The Neuronpedia survey (A.5) aggregates SAEs across very different models and scales, and comparing raw L0 values across model/dictionary sizes to declare them 'too low' is methodologically shaky.
Several figures (e.g., Figure 3) are small with unclear axis labels, making it hard to read off quantitative values.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated research question: whether L0 is a neutral design choice or has a 'correct' value, with direct practical implications for the large SAE/interpretability community.

Careful toy model design with ground-truth features allows clean causal claims; notably, the control experiment initializing the SAE at the ground-truth solution (Sec 3.1) convincingly rules out local-minimum explanations, and Sec 3.3/3.4 quantitatively show the MSE objective actively prefers feature-mixing solutions (MSE 2.73 vs 4.88).

The finding that a ground-truth SAE scores worse on reconstruction than a feature-mixing SAE at low L0 (Fig 4-5) is a genuinely important and novel critique of standard sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff evaluation.

The proposed proxy metric (nth decoder projection) is validated in multiple ways: minimized at true L0 in toy models across architectures (BatchTopK and JumpReLU), and its 'elbow' aligns with peak k-sparse probing performance on two LLMs across multiple layers and seeds.

Rich supplementary analyses: L0 transitions during training showing asymmetric recoverability (Appendix A.4), an automatic L0 optimization procedure with a candid account of its failure modes (A.6), JumpReLU vs BatchTopK threshold dynamics (A.10), and a survey of open-source SAE L0s (A.7).
Honest limitations discussion (A.8) and candid acknowledgment that the metric is not perfect, e.g., inconsistent global-minimum behavior at high L0.
weaknesses: Evidence in real LLMs is limited to a few layers of two models (Gemma-2-2b layers 5/12, Llama-3.2-1b layer 7); the headline claim that 'most commonly used SAEs have too low an L0' rests on a self-described 'cursory search' of Neuronpedia plus this limited sweep, which is thin support for such a field-wide claim.

The proxy metric is heuristic: the choice of n is justified only empirically (n near h/2 'seems to work'), the metric's high-L0 behavior is inconsistent across models and layers (sometimes no global minimum at the elbow), and no theoretical analysis is given for when it should work.

Validation of the 'correct L0' via sparse probing is somewhat circular and weak: probing F1 curves are quite flat over a wide L0 range, so 'peak performance' is imprecisely localized, and sparse probing is itself an imperfect proxy for feature correctness (as the authors' own related-work citations note SAEs underperform supervised baselines).

The central claim that sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff plots are unsound is demonstrated rigorously only in the toy model where ground truth is available; in LLMs, the paper cannot directly show that low-L0 SAEs have incorrect features beyond correlation with probing.

The toy setup assumes orthogonal features and exact linear superposition (LRH), which sidesteps non-linear features and hierarchical/absorption structures known to matter; the implications for realistic feature geometry are argued informally rather than tested.

Practical utility of the metric is limited: it requires training an entire L0 sweep, and the automatic in-training optimization 'requires a lot of hyperparameter tuning to work in real LLMs,' so a practitioner gains a diagnostic rather than a solution.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: several typos and informal phrasing (e.g., 'Afterall', 'increses'), and the code link in the introduction is left incomplete ('Code is available at'), which harms reproducibility despite otherwise reasonable experimental detail.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and under-examined question in SAE research: whether L0 is a free hyperparameter or has a 'correct' value for learning disentangled features. This challenges a widespread evaluation practice (sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff plots), and the toy-model setup with known ground-truth features makes the causal claims verifiable.

The experimental design in the toy model is careful. Notably, initializing the low-L0 SAE at the ground-truth solution (Section 3.1) rules out local minima as an explanation, showing that MSE loss actively pulls the SAE away from correct latents toward feature-mixing solutions (Section 3.3). The comparison where a ground-truth SAE scores worse on variance explained than feature-mixing SAEs (Figure 4, Section 3.4) is a compelling and clean argument that the sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff can be misleading.

The proposed proxy metric (nth decoder projection, s_n^dec) is simple, cheap to compute, and is empirically validated against k-sparse probing performance on two real LLMs (Gemma-2-2b, Llama-3.2-1b) with multiple seeds, showing the 'elbow' corresponds to peak probing performance. The appendix includes substantial additional validation (alternative pairwise cosine similarity metric, JumpReLU confirmation, transitioning-L0 dynamics in A.4).

The limitations discussion (Appendix A.8) is honest and specific: non-linear features are not considered, correlation structures are simplified, and only a few layers were investigated due to compute cost. Code availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central practical claim — 'most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low' — is under-supported. The evidence is a 'cursory search' of Neuronpedia (Appendix A.7) showing common L0 values below 100, compared against an inferred optimal L0 of 200–250 established for only a small number of layers of two models. The generality of the optimal-L0 claim across layers, models, and training regimes is not demonstrated, so the sweeping recommendation outpaces the evidence.

The proxy metric is heuristic and its behavior is inconsistent at high L0. For Gemma-2-2b layer 5, the metric 'never has a clear global minimum at the elbow point' (Figure 17); for JumpReLU SAEs, a clear minimum appears only at n = h/2 (Figures 18, 10); and for the pairwise cosine similarity metric, alignment with probing results differs between k=1 and k=16 (Appendix A.5.2), with the authors admitting they 'do not know if this is a meaningful difference.' The guidance reduces to 'practitioners try both metrics,' which limits the method's utility as a principled tool.

The LLM-side validation is thin relative to the framing: two models, a handful of layers, BatchTopK sweeps of 500M–1B tokens, and probing peak differences in F1 that are small (roughly 0.78–0.84) and identified visually via the 'elbow' rather than by a defined decision procedure. It is not shown that using the metric to select L0 reliably outperforms standard practice on downstream tasks beyond sparse probing.

The toy model's assumptions (strictly orthogonal features, correlated Bernoulli firing, exact LRH additive structure) are idealized, and the paper does not probe how robust the mixing phenomenon is to deviations from these assumptions (e.g., feature hierarchies, near-linear dependence, magnitude distributions). The mechanistic claim that low-L0 latents constitute an inescapable local minimum (Appendix A.4) is supported by a single experiment.

The proposed automatic L0 optimization (Appendix A.6) 'requires a lot of hyperparameter tuning to work in real LLMs, limiting its utility' by the authors' own admission, which weakens the practical payoff of the otherwise interesting metric.

Some quantitative rigor is missing: e.g., Section 3.3's MSE comparison (2.73 vs 4.88) uses a single configuration without error bars or seed variance, and the sparsity–reconstruction critique, while demonstrated in the toy model, is not quantified on real LLMs where ground truth is unavailable.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored question: whether L0 in SAE training is a 'free' hyperparameter or has a correct value. The finding that too-low L0 causes feature hedging/mixing, and that sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff plots can actively mislead (the ground-truth SAE scores worse than corrupted SAEs, Sec 3.4, Fig 4), is a valuable corrective to common SAE evaluation practice.

The toy-model methodology is well designed: using synthetic data with known ground-truth features, and initializing an SAE at the ground-truth solution (Sec 3.1), allows causal claims about gradient pressure rather than local minima. The MSE comparison (Sec 3.3, MSE 2.73 for incorrect latents vs 4.88 for ground truth) cleanly demonstrates that the loss itself incentivizes mixing.

Findings are validated beyond toy models on two real LLMs (Gemma-2-2b, Llama-3.2-1b), and the proposed s_dec_n metric's 'elbow' coincides with peak k-sparse probing performance (Fig 9), which is a meaningful external validation.

The paper covers both BatchTopK and JumpReLU architectures, includes an interesting per-latent L0 heterogeneity analysis (Sec 4.2) and JumpReLU-vs-BatchTopK threshold dynamics (Appendix A.10), and includes the honest observation that low-L0 states are hard local minima that the SAE cannot recover from (Appendix A.4), which has direct practical consequences.

Reproducibility is good: standard tooling (SAELens), explicit hyperparameters in the appendix, analysis of open-source SAE L0s on Neuronpedia, and code availability. The limitations section (A.8) is candid about scope (linear features only, few layers) without overclaiming.
weaknesses: The central LLM claim—that most SAEs have an L0 that is too low and that there is a 'correct' L0—rests on an unverifiable premise. Unlike the toy models, there is no ground truth in real LLMs; validation relies on correlation with sparse probing peak, which is shown for only a few layers of two models. The claim that sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff plots are 'not a sound method of evaluating SAEs' is demonstrated rigorously only in settings where ground truth exists, and the extrapolation to real SAEs is plausible but not proven.

The proposed s_dec_n metric behaves inconsistently at high L0: in some cases the global minimum appears in a long shallow region away from the 'elbow' (Gemma layer 5, Sec 4), and for JumpReLU a clear minimum appears only at n = h/2 (Sec 4.1, A.9). The authors honestly note the metric is 'not a perfect guide,' but this ambiguity weakens the metric's practical utility and the precision of the claimed optimal L0.

The metric requires training a full sweep of SAEs across L0 values, which is expensive; the proposed automatic optimization during training (A.6) is acknowledged to require extensive hyperparameter tuning and 'limits its utility' in real LLMs, so the paper's actionable output for practitioners is limited.

The work is a fairly incremental extension of Chanin et al. (2025) on feature hedging—here attributed to too-low L0 rather than narrow SAEs—plus a new heuristic metric. The related-work positioning is fair, but the conceptual novelty is moderate.

Toy model assumptions (perfectly orthogonal linear features, correlated Bernoulli firing, no superposition/nonlinear features) are strong idealizations; while the limitations are discussed, the gap between these assumptions and real LLM activation structure is nontrivial, and only a handful of layers were examined due to cost.
